stem: An 18-year-old tall woman has never menstruated. Her breasts are normal, but she has almost no pubic or axillary hair. Examination shows a blind-ending vagina, and ultrasound finds no uterus. Palpable masses lie in both inguinal canals. LH and testosterone are high.
oneliner: 18F + tall + primary amenorrhea + normal breasts + no pubic/axillary hair + blind vagina + no uterus + inguinal masses + high LH and T → karyotype?
ask: Which karyotype does she most likely have?

whyNot.A: **Turner syndrome**: short stature, streak ovaries and a **uterus present**, with no testes in the inguinal canals
whyNot.B: A 46,XX woman with no uterus (MRKH) has **normal pubic hair, ovaries and female-range testosterone**, with no testes
whyNot.D: A Turner variant: **short stature and streak gonads**, not tall with testes and high testosterone
whyNot.E: **Klinefelter**: a male phenotype with small firm testes, gynecomastia and a normal male tract, not a blind vagina

why: Testes make **normal-to-high testosterone and AMH**, so the Mullerian structures (uterus, tubes, upper vagina) regress. The **defective androgen receptor** blocks pubic and axillary hair and male genitalia, while peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogen gives normal breasts.

idea.rule: 46,XY with a female phenotype and no uterus means the testes made AMH but androgen action failed.
also: Partial AIS: some receptor function gives ambiguous genitalia, still no uterus
5-alpha-reductase deficiency: AMH and testosterone work, only DHT fails, so no uterus and ambiguous genitalia
Testicular feminization is the old name for complete AIS

stem: A 25-year-old woman at 12 weeks of gestation passes tissue per vagina. Pathology shows an identifiable fetus, focal swelling of the villi, and mild trophoblastic proliferation. Fetal red cells are seen in villous vessels. The karyotype of the tissue is 69,XXY, and her beta-hCG is only moderately raised.
oneliner: 25F + 12 wk + passes tissue with fetal parts + focal villous swelling + fetal red cells + 69,XXY + modest hCG → what fertilization event?
ask: Which event most likely produced this conceptus?

options.A: A normal ovum fertilized by two sperm
options.B: An empty ovum fertilized by one sperm that duplicates
options.D: Failure to extrude the second polar body
options.E: Postzygotic loss of a chromosome (trisomy rescue)

whyNot.B: That gives a **complete mole**: 46,XX paternal only, **no fetal parts** and diffuse swelling
whyNot.C: Gives a **trisomy or monosomy** (diploid-range count), not a **triploid 69** set
whyNot.D: Gives a **digynic** triploid (two maternal sets) with a small non-molar placenta; **focal villous swelling and trophoblast proliferation** need **two paternal sets**
whyNot.E: Removes a chromosome (**mosaicism or uniparental disomy**); it cannot create 69 chromosomes

answer: One normal ovum fertilized by two sperm (dispermy)
why: Two sperm add **two paternal haploid sets** to one maternal set, giving **triploid 69,XXY**; the **Y must come from a sperm**. The surviving fetal tissue explains the **partial mole**, with focal villous change and a lower hCG than a complete mole.

idea.rule: Count the parental chromosome sets: partial mole is 1 maternal + 2 paternal, complete mole is 0 maternal + 2 paternal.
also: Complete mole: 46,XX, all paternal, no fetal tissue
Triploidy is lethal; the rare fetus is severely growth restricted
Partial mole has a low risk of choriocarcinoma

stem: A 19-year-old woman at 10 weeks of gestation has vaginal spotting. Her uterus reaches the umbilicus, and beta-hCG is 350,000 mIU/mL. Ultrasound shows no fetal parts. Villi are diffusely swollen with circumferential trophoblastic proliferation, and the tissue is 46,XX with all chromosomes paternal.
oneliner: 19F + 10 wk + spotting + uterus to umbilicus + hCG 350,000 + no fetal parts + diffuse swollen villi + 46,XX all paternal → what event?
ask: Which event most likely produced this tissue?

options.A: One normal ovum fertilized by two sperm
options.C: Failure to extrude the second polar body
options.D: Fertilization of a normal ovum by one diploid sperm
options.E: An empty ovum plus one duplicated sperm

whyNot.A: That makes a **partial mole**: triploid 69, with **fetal parts** and focal change
whyNot.B: Gives a **trisomy**; it does not remove all maternal DNA, and the tissue here is **all paternal**
whyNot.C: Adds **maternal** chromosomes, but this tissue has **none**
whyNot.D: Would give **triploid 69** with maternal DNA present, not a 46,XX tissue of purely paternal origin

answer: An empty ovum fertilized by one sperm that duplicates (androgenesis)
why: An ovum with **no maternal DNA** is fertilized by one sperm whose genome **duplicates**, giving **46,XX, all paternal**. No embryo forms, so there are **no fetal parts**, villi swell diffusely, and **hCG is very high**.

idea.rule: Complete mole = paternal only with no fetus; partial mole = triploid with a fetus.
also: Complete mole: higher risk of choriocarcinoma
Theca lutein cysts from very high hCG
